pos: n. (one who tempts or solicits to evil; by eminence, Satan)
etymology: From tempt, Latin tentare, to try, to test, to attempt. In English the word narrowed from testing to soliciting to evil; Scripture keeps both senses distinct and assigns them to different persons.
biblical_def: Twice the Authorized Version names a person the tempter, and both times it means Satan. The first is in the wilderness: “And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread” (Mat 4:3). The second is Paul's anxiety over a young church under persecution: “I sent to know your faith, lest by some means the tempter have tempted you, and our labour be in vain” (1Th 3:5). The title is a job description. He does not merely accuse and he does not merely deceive; he solicits, and he solicits at the point of legitimate need — a hungry man and bread, a harassed church and relief. Scripture is careful to keep the office out of God's hands entirely: “Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man” (Jas 1:13). God tests; He does not solicit to evil. And the comfort of the doctrine is that the tempter met his match in a hungry Man: our high priest “was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” (Heb 4:15). Christ was not spared the assault; He endured it whole and unbroken, which is why He can help those who are under it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tempter as one who tempts or entices to evil; and, by way of eminence, the great tempter of mankind, Satan or the devil.
webster_full: TEMPT'ER, n.
1. One that tempts or entices; as a tempter to vice.
2. The great tempter of mankind; Satan; the devil.
So glozed the tempter, and his proem tuned.
The word is from the Latin tentare, to try or attempt; in Scripture the trying that solicits to evil is never ascribed to God.
scriptures: Matthew 4:3
And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread.
1 Thessalonians 3:5
For this cause, when I could no longer forbear, I sent to know your faith, lest by some means the tempter have tempted you, and our labour be in vain.
James 1:13
Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man:
Hebrews 4:15
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
corruption_summary: The tempter has been dissolved into a metaphor for internal drives, which removes the enemy and leaves the sin unexplained.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberal theology long ago demythologized the tempter into a personification of human impulse, and much popular evangelicalism has quietly agreed by simply never mentioning him. The cost is not merely a lost doctrine but a lost account of what is happening. 1 Thessalonians 3:5 shows an apostle sending a man on a long journey because he was afraid of a person, not of a psychological tendency. Remove that person and Christian struggle becomes a purely internal affair, which is precisely the conclusion the therapeutic register wants: what Scripture calls temptation becomes a pattern to be managed rather than an assault to be resisted.

The opposite corruption over-supplies the devil and under-supplies responsibility, so that every sin is an attack and no sin is a choice. James guards both flanks in one chapter: the tempter is real, God is not him, and a man is drawn away of his own lust. And Matthew 4 sets the pattern for resistance — not clever debate and not an exorcism, but written Scripture quoted against a proposition that sounded reasonable to a starving man. The tempter's offer was bread. That is his method: never obviously evil, always adjacent to a real need.
roots_summary: Greek ho peirazon (G3985), the one tempting; peirasmos (G3986), trial or temptation; Hebrew satan (H7854), adversary; Latin tentare, to try.
roots_lines: Greek ho peirazon (G3985) — the tempting one, a present participle used as a title; Matthew 4:3 and 1 Thessalonians 3:5.
Greek peirasmos (G3986) — trial, testing, temptation; the same noun covers God's proving and Satan's soliciting, distinguished by who is acting.
Greek apeirastos kakon (G551) — untemptable by evil; James 1:13 of God, an absolute statement.
Hebrew satan (H7854) — adversary, accuser; the Old Testament office behind the New Testament title.
Latin tentare — to try, test, attempt; Webster's root, where the trying and the soliciting still share a word.
usage: “When the tempter came to him” — to a hungry man, about bread.
“Lest by some means the tempter have tempted you” — an apostle afraid of a person.
“God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man” — the office is not His.

pos: n. (lasciviousness; licentiousness; unrestrained indulgence of appetite)
etymology: Middle English wantowen, from wan- (lacking, as in wanting) and towen (trained, disciplined) — literally undisciplined, untrained. The English etymology is itself a sermon: wantonness is what a man does when nothing has been broken in him.
biblical_def: Wantonness is appetite off the leash. Paul lists it among the works of darkness a Christian is to put off with the night: “Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying” (Rom 13:13). The pairing is deliberate — drunkenness with rioting, wantonness with chambering — sins of the table and sins of the bed, both of them the appetite made sovereign. Peter shows how it is marketed: “when they speak great swelling words of vanity, they allure through the lusts of the flesh, through much wantonness, those that were clean escaped from them who live in error” (2Pe 2:18). Notice who the targets are. False teachers aim wantonness at recent converts — men clean escaped — and the bait is offered with swelling words, that is, with a rhetoric of freedom. Jude names the same trade in one phrase: “turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness” (Jud 1:4). Grace is the very thing twisted into the licence. And Paul is blunt that none of this is obscure or disputable: “the works of the flesh are manifest” (Gal 5:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wantonness as sportiveness; negligence of restraint; lasciviousness; lecherousness; and licentiousness of manners.
webster_full: WAN'TONNESS, n.
1. Sportiveness; gayety; frolicsomeness; waggery.
2. Licentiousness; negligence of restraint.
The tumults threatened to abuse all acts of grace, and turn them into wantonness.
3. Lasciviousness; lecherousness. Not in chambering and wantonness. Rom. 13. The word is from wan, wanting, and towen, trained; that is, untrained, undisciplined.
scriptures: Romans 13:13
Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.
2 Peter 2:18
For when they speak great swelling words of vanity, they allure through the lusts of the flesh, through much wantonness, those that were clean escaped from them who live in error.
Jude 1:4

For there are certain men crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ.
Galatians 5:19
Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness,
corruption_summary: Wantonness is now called liberation, and the rebranding is done, as Peter said it would be, with swelling words about freedom.
corruption_paragraphs: The sexual revolution did not invent a new sin; it renamed an old one. What Romans 13:13 calls chambering and wantonness is now described as self-expression, exploration, or authenticity — and the change of vocabulary does all the work that argument could not. 2 Peter 2:18 predicted the technique exactly: great swelling words of vanity, deployed to allure. The words are inflated on purpose, because the thing itself cannot be commended plainly. When a practice needs a grand word to be acceptable, the grand word is the evidence.

Jude 1:4 identifies the aggravated form, which is peculiar to the church: turning the grace of God into lasciviousness. This is antinomianism, and it is not the doctrine of grace pressed too far but grace inverted into its opposite — the argument that since sin is forgiven it is therefore indifferent. Romans 6 answers it with the horror it deserves. The Reformed position holds both ends without flinching: justification is by faith alone, and the faith that justifies is never alone, because the same Spirit who applies Christ's righteousness also puts the appetite back under discipline. Wantonness is untrainedness; sanctification is the training.
roots_summary: Greek aselgeia (G766), licentiousness, shameless excess; koite (G2845), bed, chambering; Middle English wantowen, untrained.
roots_lines: Greek aselgeia (G766) — unbridled shamelessness, licentiousness; rendered wantonness in Romans 13:13 and lasciviousness in Galatians 5:19 and Jude 4.
Greek koitais (G2845) — beds; the chambering Paul pairs with wantonness, and the root of English coitus.
Greek huperonka mataiotetos (G5246, G3153) — great swelling words of emptiness; 2 Peter 2:18, the rhetoric of the sale.
Greek deleazousin (G1185) — they bait, as a hook is baited; the verb behind allure.
Middle English wan- and towen — lacking training; the English etymology is itself the definition.
usage: “Not in chambering and wantonness” — the appetite made sovereign, at table and in bed.
“Great swelling words of vanity” — when a practice needs a grand word, the word is the evidence.
“Turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness” — the aggravated, churchly form.

pos: n. (extreme wickedness; baseness of conduct; a vile act)
etymology: Old French vilenie, from vilain, a serf or peasant attached to a villa — the word's descent from a social class to a moral judgment is one of the ugliest in English. Scripture, by contrast, uses it strictly of conduct.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version spells it with one l and uses it twice, both for wickedness that has stopped hiding. Isaiah places it in a prophecy about the day when names will finally match things: “The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful” (Isa 32:5), and then “For the vile person will speak villany, and his heart will work iniquity, to practise hypocrisy, and to utter error against the LORD, to make empty the soul of the hungry, and he will cause the drink of the thirsty to fail” (Isa 32:6). Read the sequence: speech, then heart, then hypocrisy, then error against God, then the hungry go empty. Isaiah traces villany from the mouth to the stomach of a poor man, and insists the two ends are the same sin. Jeremiah's use is equally concrete: the false prophets “have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours' wives, and have spoken lying words in my name” (Jer 29:23). Again the pattern — adultery and false prophecy named in one breath, because a man who will lie about God will lie about anything. Villany in Scripture is never merely a private vice; it always reaches somebody.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines villany as extreme depravity; atrocious wickedness; and an act of deep depravity.
webster_full: VIL'LANY, n. [from villain.]
1. Extreme depravity; atrocious wickedness.
2. An act of deep depravity.
To fill the measure of thy villanies.
3. The act of a villain; a crime. The vile person will speak villany. Isa. 32. The word descends from villain, originally a feudal tenant, and became a moral term by the world's contempt.
scriptures: Isaiah 32:6

For the vile person will speak villany, and his heart will work iniquity, to practise hypocrisy, and to utter error against the LORD, to make empty the soul of the hungry, and he will cause the drink of the thirsty to fail.
Jeremiah 29:23

Because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours' wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them; even I know, and am a witness, saith the LORD.
Isaiah 32:5
The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful.
Proverbs 6:12
A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth.
corruption_summary: The age has abolished the category of the villain, keeping only the categories of the sick and the misunderstood.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary moral vocabulary has almost no room left for villany. Wickedness is reclassified as pathology, upbringing, or systemic effect, and the man himself becomes a site where causes met. There is a real truth being abused here — sin does have a history, and providence does place men in circumstances. But Isaiah 32:6 locates the engine in the heart: his heart will work iniquity. Remove that and you have removed the possibility of repentance along with the possibility of guilt, and the man who is only a product cannot be forgiven, because there is no one there to forgive.

Isaiah 32:5 names the opposite corruption and it is the one the prophet expects to last longest: the vile person called liberal, the churl said to be bountiful. Wickedness with a good press. The day of the Lord is described in part as the day the labels come off. Until then the church's duty is the unfashionable one of calling things by their names, which is why the Reformed pulpit has always preached the law before the gospel — not to produce despair, but because a man who has never been told he is a villain has never been told the truth he needs in order to be saved.
roots_summary: Hebrew nebalah (H5039), senseless wickedness, disgraceful folly; nabal (H5036), fool, vile person; Old French vilenie.
roots_lines: Hebrew nebalah (H5039) — disgraceful folly, outrage; the word for Dinah's violation in Genesis 34:7 and for villany in Isaiah 32:6.
Hebrew nabal (H5036) — the fool, the vile person; the same root that names Abigail's husband, and Abigail says the name fits.
Hebrew aven (H205) — iniquity, trouble; his heart will work iniquity, Isaiah 32:6.
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood; the lying words spoken in the LORD's name, Jeremiah 29:23.
Old French vilenie, from vilain — a villa-tenant; a class term that the world turned into a moral one.
usage: “The vile person will speak villany” — and the hungry soul goes empty; one sin, both ends.
“Shall be no more called liberal” — the day the labels come off.
“Committed adultery… and have spoken lying words in my name” — named together, and rightly.

pos: n. pl. (contemptuous or abusive speech; reproaches)
etymology: From revile, Old French reviler, to hold cheap, from re- and vil, vile — literally to make vile, to treat a man as worthless by speech.
biblical_def: Revilings are words used as weapons, and the Authorized Version records God's attention to them twice. The first is a command to a persecuted remnant: “Hearken unto me, ye that know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear ye not the reproach of men, neither be ye afraid of their revilings” (Isa 51:7). The people addressed are marked by the law being in the heart, and what they are told is not to answer, argue, or out-shout, but not to be afraid. The second shows why: “I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the revilings of the children of Ammon, whereby they have reproached my people, and magnified themselves against their border” (Zep 2:8). God has been listening the whole time, and the reviling of His people is filed as an offence against Him. The Christian's pattern is his Lord: “Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1Pe 2:23). And the reviled are pronounced blessed rather than pitied: “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” (Mat 5:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reviling as reproaching; treating with opprobrious language; and as a noun, the act of vilifying, reproachful language.
webster_full: REVI'LING, ppr. Reproaching; treating with opprobrious or contemptuous language.
REVI'LING, n. The act of vilifying; reproachful language; contemptuous speech.
Neither be ye afraid of their revilings. Isa. 51.
To revile is from re and vile; that is, to make vile, to treat as worthless.
Revilers are ranked in Scripture with the covetous and the extortioners. 1 Cor. 6.
scriptures: Isaiah 51:7
Hearken unto me, ye that know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear ye not the reproach of men, neither be ye afraid of their revilings.
Zephaniah 2:8
I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the revilings of the children of Ammon, whereby they have reproached my people, and magnified themselves against their border.
1 Peter 2:23
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
Matthew 5:11
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
corruption_summary: Reviling has been industrialized by the network age, and the church has largely joined in rather than absorbed it.
corruption_paragraphs: Every age has revilers; this one has given them a distribution system, a scoreboard, and an income. The machinery rewards contempt because contempt performs, and the result is a public square in which making another man vile is a career. Isaiah 51:7 speaks directly to those under it and says a surprising thing: not answer them but fear them not. The fear is the real damage. A church that is afraid of revilings will trim its preaching long before anyone lays a hand on it, which is why the command is addressed precisely to the people who have the law in their heart.

The graver failure is the church reviling back. 1 Peter 2:23 records that Christ, who had every fact on His side and infinite power in reserve, reviled not again — and the reason given is not that He was above it but that He committed himself to him that judgeth righteously. Non-retaliation is an act of faith in a real coming judgment, not a strategy of niceness. Where that judgment is doubted, believers take their own case in hand and answer contempt with contempt. 1 Peter 3:9 forbids it plainly: not railing for railing, but contrariwise blessing.
roots_summary: Hebrew gidduph (H1421), reviling, reproach; Greek loidoreo (G3058), to revile, to abuse; Old French reviler, to make vile.
roots_lines: Hebrew gidduphotam (H1421) — their revilings, blasphemies; Isaiah 51:7, and the same root is used of blasphemy against God.
Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach, scorn; paired with revilings in both Isaiah 51:7 and Zephaniah 2:8.
Greek loidoroumenos ouk anteloidorei (G3058) — being reviled, He reviled not in return; 1 Peter 2:23.
Greek oneidisosin (G3679) — they shall reproach; Matthew 5:11, where the reviled are called blessed.
Old French reviler, from vil — to make vile; the etymology names the intent exactly.
usage: “Neither be ye afraid of their revilings” — not answer them; fear them not.
“I have heard the reproach of Moab” — He has been listening the whole time.
“Reviled not again… but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” — restraint resting on a real judgment.

pos: n. (the quality of being slothful; sluggishness; idleness; habitual indolence)
etymology: From slothful, from sloth, Saxon slaewth, from slaw, slow. English named the animal after the vice, not the vice after the animal.
biblical_def: Solomon and the Preacher each give the word once, and between them they describe the whole career of the sluggard — what it does to the man, and what it does to his house. Inward first: “Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep; and an idle soul shall suffer hunger” (Pro 19:15). It is not merely that the slothful man sleeps; slothfulness casts him into sleep, deepening its own hold, and the end is hunger — a natural consequence, not an arbitrary punishment. Then outward: “By much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through” (Ecc 10:18). Nobody demolishes the house. It simply is not maintained, and a roof left alone lets the rain in. That is the characteristic mark of this sin: it destroys by omission, which is why it so rarely feels like sin at the time. Solomon puts it in company that should sting: “He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster” (Pro 18:9) — the idle man and the squanderer are family. Paul makes the same judgment a rule of church order: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines slothfulness as the indulgence of sloth; inactivity; the habit of idleness; laziness.
webster_full: SLOTH'FULNESS, n.
The indulgence of sloth; inactivity; the habit of idleness; laziness.
Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep. Prov. 19.
By much slothfulness the building decayeth. Eccles. 10.
Sloth is from the Saxon slaewth, from slaw, slow; the beast was named from the vice.
scriptures: Proverbs 19:15
Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep; and an idle soul shall suffer hunger.
Ecclesiastes 10:18
By much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through.
Proverbs 18:9
He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster.
2 Thessalonians 3:10
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
corruption_summary: Slothfulness now travels under better names — rest, boundaries, self-care — and the sin that destroys by omission has found the perfect vocabulary.
corruption_paragraphs: This is the sin most easily laundered, because its outward form is indistinguishable from a virtue the Bible actually commands. Scripture prescribes rest: a sabbath, sleep as a gift, a Christ who told tired apostles to come apart and rest a while. The wellness vocabulary of the moment supplies a set of terms — self-care, boundaries, protecting one's peace — that can describe either genuine rest or plain sloth without distinguishing them. Ecclesiastes 10:18 provides the test, and it is an external one: look at the roof. Slothfulness is identified not by how tired a man feels but by what has quietly stopped being maintained — the house, the work, the family worship, the neglected duty.

There is a second corruption that runs the other way, and the Reformed have been more prone to it: treating busyness as righteousness, so that a man who is never still assumes he is never slothful. Proverbs 19:15 says an idle soul shall suffer hunger, and a soul can be idle while the calendar is full. The Puritan doctrine of vocation cuts both ways — it dignifies ordinary labour as service to God, and it therefore refuses to count frantic motion as diligence. The question is not how much a man does but whether the work God actually gave him is being done.
roots_summary: Hebrew atslah (H6103), sluggishness; atsel (H6102), sluggard; Greek okneros (G3636), slothful; Saxon slaw, slow.
roots_lines: Hebrew atslah (H6103) — sluggishness, laziness; Proverbs 19:15 and Ecclesiastes 10:18, the only two places the noun appears.
Hebrew atsel (H6102) — the sluggard; the figure Proverbs sends to the ant in 6:6.
Hebrew mithrappeh (H7503) — slack, letting the hands drop; Proverbs 18:9, brother to the waster.
Greek okneros (G3636) — shrinking, slothful; the wicked and slothful servant of Matthew 25:26.
Saxon slaewth, from slaw, slow — Webster's root; the animal was named afterward.
usage: “Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep” — the sin deepens its own hold.
“The building decayeth… the house droppeth through” — nobody demolished it.
“Brother to him that is a great waster” — the idle man and the squanderer are family.

pos: adv. (with spite or malice; malignantly; with intent to injure)
etymology: From spiteful, from spite, a contraction of despite, from Latin despicere, to look down upon. Spite is contempt turned into action — injury done for the pleasure of doing it.
biblical_def: The adverb appears twice, and both times describes how messengers of God are handled. The first is in the parable of the marriage feast: “And the remnant took his servants, and entreated them spitefully, and slew them” (Mat 22:6). The servants brought an invitation to a wedding; the response was torture and murder. Nothing in the errand provoked it, which is the point — spite does not require a cause, only an occasion. The second is the Lord's own prediction of His passion: “For he shall be delivered unto the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on” (Luk 18:32). Christ names the treatment before He receives it, and the list is not of legal penalties but of humiliations: mocking, spite, spitting. These add nothing to the execution; they exist purely to degrade. So Scripture puts the word twice where the gospel is being carried and twice where it is answered with malice, and then commands the opposite from those who suffer it: “pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you” (Mat 5:44), and “not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing” (1Pe 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spitefully as with spite; malignantly; with desire to vex, annoy or injure; malignly.
webster_full: SPI'TEFULLY, adv.
With spite; malignantly; with desire to vex, annoy or injure; malignly.
They took his servants and entreated them spitefully. Matt. 22.
Spite is a contraction of despite, from the Latin despicere, to look down upon or despise.
It denotes a malignant desire of injuring another, without provocation proportioned to the act.
scriptures: Matthew 22:6
And the remnant took his servants, and entreated them spitefully, and slew them.
Luke 18:32
For he shall be delivered unto the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on:
Matthew 5:44
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
1 Peter 3:9
Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing.
corruption_summary: Spite is the one motive the modern account of human nature cannot accommodate, so it is renamed as grievance and thereby justified.
corruption_paragraphs: Every secular anthropology assumes men act from interest — they seek advantage, security, or relief. Spite breaks the model, because spite will pay to hurt. Matthew 22:6 describes men who gained absolutely nothing by torturing a wedding messenger. The Reformed doctrine of total depravity is the only account that predicts this without embarrassment: the fallen will is not merely misinformed about its own good, it is hostile, and hostility does not need a profit motive. Where that doctrine is abandoned, spite must be re-explained as a response to injury — and so every spiteful act acquires a justifying history and becomes a grievance.

Luke 18:32 shows the same malice reaching its object. The spitting added nothing to the crucifixion; it was gratuitous, and the Son of God foretold it among the things He would receive. That is where the command in Matthew 5:44 gets its force. Praying for those who despitefully use you is not a technique for de-escalation and not an assertion that the malice is imaginary — the Lord names it plainly and then says pray. Blessing in return is possible only because a righteous Judge has the case (1Pe 2:23), which is precisely the doctrine the reviling age has lost.
roots_summary: Greek hubrizo (G5195), to treat insolently, outrage; epereazo (G1908), to use despitefully; Latin despicere, to look down upon.
roots_lines: Greek hubrisan (G5195) — they outraged, treated with insolence; Matthew 22:6 and Luke 18:32, the root of English hubris.
Greek epereazonton (G1908) — those who use despitefully, who threaten and abuse; Matthew 5:44.
Greek emptusthesetai (G1716) — He shall be spat upon; Luke 18:32, a humiliation adding nothing to the sentence.
Greek loidorian anti loidorias (G3059) — railing for railing; 1 Peter 3:9, forbidden outright.
Latin despicere — to look down upon; Webster's root, contempt before it becomes injury.
usage: “Entreated them spitefully, and slew them” — over a wedding invitation.
“Mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on” — foretold, and none of it added to the sentence.
“Pray for them which despitefully use you” — named plainly, then prayed for.

pos: adv. (in an unjust manner; wrongfully; contrary to right or law)
etymology: From unjust, Latin injustus, from in- (not) and justus, just, from jus, right, law. The adverb describes not merely a wrong outcome but a wrong manner of judging.
biblical_def: Both occurrences concern judgment. The first is God arraigning the judges themselves: “How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah” (Psa 82:2). Psalm 82 has God standing in the congregation of the mighty and putting magistrates on trial — the ones who hold the bench are themselves before a bench. And the specific charge is accepting persons: deciding cases by who the man is rather than what the case is. That is the Bible's standing definition of injustice, and it cuts equally against favouring the rich and favouring the poor, since Leviticus forbids both. The second occurrence exposes something darker — that injustice survives kindness: “Let favour be shewed to the wicked, yet will he not learn righteousness: in the land of uprightness will he deal unjustly, and will not behold the majesty of the LORD” (Isa 26:10). Mercy alone does not reform a man; grace must change the heart or the wicked will practise injustice in the very land of uprightness. The law is blunt about the mechanism: “a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous” (Deu 16:19), and about the verdict: “He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD” (Pro 17:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unjustly as in an unjust manner; wrongfully; in violation of right, law or justice.
webster_full: UNJUST'LY, adv.
In an unjust manner; wrongfully.
How long will ye judge unjustly? Ps. 82.
In violation of the rules of justice; as, to condemn a man unjustly.
From the Latin injustus, from in, not, and justus, just, from jus, right or law.
scriptures: Psalm 82:2
How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah.
Isaiah 26:10
Let favour be shewed to the wicked, yet will he not learn righteousness: in the land of uprightness will he deal unjustly, and will not behold the majesty of the LORD.
Deuteronomy 16:19
Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.
Proverbs 17:15
He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.
corruption_summary: Justice has been redefined from judging a case by its merits to adjusting outcomes by group — which is exactly the respecting of persons the law forbids.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture's definition of injustice is precise and portable: accepting persons, judging a case by who the parties are. Deuteronomy 16:19 forbids wresting judgment and respecting persons in one breath, and Leviticus 19:15 closes the obvious loophole by forbidding partiality toward the poor as well as deference to the mighty. Any framework that assigns guilt or innocence, credibility or suspicion, by category rather than by evidence has therefore adopted the very thing Psalm 82 arraigns — whichever direction it tilts. The biblical categories for the wronged are real and God attends to them: the widow, the fatherless, the stranger, the hired man whose wages are withheld. They are categories of actual wrong suffered, not of standing assigned in advance.

Isaiah 26:10 blocks the opposite error, which is the belief that injustice is only ever the fruit of hard circumstances, so that improving conditions will produce righteousness. Show the wicked favour, the prophet says, and he still will not learn righteousness — he will deal unjustly in the land of uprightness itself. That is total depravity applied to social policy. It does not excuse the church from doing justice; it explains why doing justice never finishes, and why the only final remedy is the new heart. Proverbs 17:15 then names the ultimate perversion: justifying the wicked and condemning the just — and it is worth noting that the gospel does justify the ungodly, but only because the Just One was condemned in their place, so that God might be just and the justifier.
roots_summary: Hebrew avel (H5766), injustice, unrighteousness; nasa panim (H5375, H6440), to lift the face, to accept persons; Latin injustus.
roots_lines: Hebrew avel (H5766) — injustice, perversity; Psalm 82:2, to judge injustice as a manner of judging.
Hebrew nasa penei rasha'im (H5375, H6440) — to lift the faces of the wicked; the idiom the Authorized Version renders accept the persons.
Hebrew ye'avvel (H5765) — he will act unjustly; Isaiah 26:10, in the land of uprightness itself.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, the just verdict; what Deuteronomy 16:19 forbids wresting.
Latin jus, justus, injustus — right, just, unjust; Webster's root.
usage: “How long will ye judge unjustly” — spoken to the bench, from a higher bench.
“Accept the persons of the wicked” — the Bible's standing definition of injustice.
“In the land of uprightness will he deal unjustly” — conditions do not make righteousness.

pos: adv. (in a corrupt manner; viciously; with depravity; contrary to purity)
etymology: From corrupt, Latin corrumpere, to break to pieces, to spoil, from con- and rumpere, to break. Corruption in the root sense is not filth added but soundness broken.
biblical_def: Twice the Authorized Version uses the adverb, and the two places show the sin at its two levels — the nation's and the penitent's. The first is the verdict on Jotham's reign: “And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah did: howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD. And the people did yet corruptly” (2Ch 27:2). It is one of the saddest sentences in Chronicles. A genuinely good king, careful where his father had presumed, and the people go on corrupting anyway. A righteous magistrate cannot make a people holy; reformation from the throne reaches only so deep. The second is Nehemiah on his knees: “We have dealt very corruptly against thee, and have not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the judgments, which thou commandedst thy servant Moses” (Neh 1:7). Note the pronoun. Nehemiah was in Persia, a boy or unborn when the walls fell, and he says we. That is covenantal confession, and it is the posture that actually precedes rebuilding. The root of the whole matter is stated at the flood: “God looked upon the earth, and, behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth” (Gen 6:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines corruptly as in a corrupt manner; with corruption; viciously; wickedly; by bribery.
webster_full: CORRUPT'LY, adv.
In a corrupt manner; viciously; wickedly; without integrity.
We have dealt very corruptly against thee. Neh. 1.
By bribes; by means of corruption; as a judge who decides corruptly.
From the Latin corrumpere, to break in pieces, to spoil; con and rumpo, to break.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 27:2
And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah did: howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD. And the people did yet corruptly.
Nehemiah 1:7
We have dealt very corruptly against thee, and have not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the judgments, which thou commandedst thy servant Moses.
Genesis 6:12
And God looked upon the earth, and, behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth.
Proverbs 17:15
He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.
corruption_summary: Corruption is treated as a problem of systems to be re-engineered rather than of hearts to be renewed, and so reform never reaches the thing that is broken.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Chronicles 27:2 is the permanent rebuke to political messianism in every century. Jotham did right; he was more careful than his father; and the people did yet corruptly. Scripture records good administration and continued corruption in the same verse without treating it as a contradiction, because the throne governs conduct and cannot govern the heart. Christians who have staked everything on capturing an office, and Christians who despair because the office was lost, are both reading this verse as though it could not be true. The civil magistrate is a real ordinance of God with a real sphere; it has never been a means of grace.

Nehemiah 1:7 supplies what the age finds hardest — a confession in the first person plural by a man who could plausibly have used the third. Modern discourse about corruption is almost entirely accusatory: it is always they who have dealt corruptly, and the speaker's role is diagnosis. Nehemiah names himself and his father's house before he asks for anything, and it is from that posture that the walls actually go up. Genesis 6:12 explains why the plural is honest: all flesh had corrupted his way, and the Reformed doctrine of original sin is simply this verse read without flinching.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachath (H7843), to spoil, ruin, corrupt; chabal (H2254), to act corruptly, to bind in pledge; Latin corrumpere, to break in pieces.
roots_lines: Hebrew chabol chabalnu (H2254) — corrupting we have corrupted; Nehemiah 1:7, the doubled verb the Authorized Version renders very corruptly.
Hebrew shachath (H7843) — to spoil, to ruin, to destroy; Genesis 6:12, all flesh had corrupted its way.
Hebrew mashchith (H4889) — a ruin, corruption; the noun from the same root, used of the destroyer.
Greek phtheiro (G5351) — to corrupt, to spoil; 1 Corinthians 15:33, evil communications corrupt good manners.
Latin corrumpere, from con- and rumpere — to break to pieces; corruption is soundness broken, not filth added.
usage: “And the people did yet corruptly” — under a good king, and the verse says both.
“We have dealt very corruptly against thee” — the pronoun is the repentance.
“All flesh had corrupted his way” — original sin stated as a survey of the earth.

pos: a. (full of wrath; very angry; and of God, expressing His settled indignation against sin)
etymology: From wrath, Saxon wraeth, from writhan, to writhe or twist — the body's convulsion under passion. English keeps the physical picture inside the moral word.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses wrathful twice, once of God and once of a man, and the difference between them is the whole doctrine. Of God: “Pour out thine indignation upon them, and let thy wrathful anger take hold of them” (Psa 69:24). This is an imprecation from a psalm the New Testament repeatedly applies to Christ, and it asks for God's anger, not the psalmist's — the petition itself is an act of restraint, handing the case upward. God's wrath is not a loss of composure; it is His holiness set against sin, settled, measured, and just. Of man: “A wrathful man stirreth up strife: but he that is slow to anger appeaseth strife” (Pro 15:18). Here wrath is simply destructive. It does not produce justice; it produces more conflict, and Solomon puts the slow-to-anger man opposite him as the one who quiets a quarrel. James states the rule flatly: “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jas 1:20), and Paul puts it on the list of things to be put away: “Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice” (Eph 4:31). The wrath that saves is God's, poured out at the cross; the wrath that ruins is ours.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wrathful as very angry; greatly incensed; and also springing from wrath, or expressing it, as a wrathful countenance.
webster_full: WRATH'FUL, a.
1. Very angry; greatly incensed.
A wrathful man stirreth up strife. Prov. 15.
2. Springing from wrath, or expressing it; as wrathful passions; a wrathful countenance.
Wrath is from the Saxon wraeth, connected with writhan, to writhe; the word carries the body's convulsion into the passion.
scriptures: Psalm 69:24
Pour out thine indignation upon them, and let thy wrathful anger take hold of them.
Proverbs 15:18
A wrathful man stirreth up strife: but he that is slow to anger appeaseth strife.
James 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
Ephesians 4:31
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:
corruption_summary: God's wrath is denied as unworthy of Him, while man's wrath is celebrated as the engine of righteousness — the exact inversion of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Progressive theology's central objection to penal substitution is that a wrathful God is a primitive God — cosmic child abuse, as the slogan has it. The objection mistakes the nature of the attribute. Divine wrath in Scripture is not temper; it is the fixed opposition of holiness to sin, and a God incapable of it would be a God indifferent to the rape of a child. Psalm 69 is quoted of Christ repeatedly in the New Testament, and the answer to its petition is finally given at Golgotha, where the wrathful anger falls on the Substitute. Remove the wrath and Calvary becomes a gesture rather than a payment. <!-- voice-lock-ok: progressive: names the objection to penal substitution in order to rebut it -->

The mirror corruption is the sanctifying of human wrath. Every faction now presents its anger as moral clarity, and a generation has been taught that indignation is the proof of conscience. James 1:20 is a single sentence and it closes the argument: the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God. Not rarely — not. Proverbs 15:18 gives the practical outcome, which is more strife, and Ephesians 4:31 puts it out of doors with bitterness and clamour. The believer who has a real injury is not told to feel nothing; he is told to hand the case to the Judge, which is what Psalm 69 itself is doing.
roots_summary: Hebrew charon aph (H2740, H639), burning of the nostril, fierce anger; chemah (H2534), heat, fury; Greek orge (G3709), settled wrath; Saxon wraeth.
roots_lines: Hebrew charon appekha (H2740, H639) — the burning of thy nostril; Psalm 69:24, the Hebrew idiom for fierce anger.
Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, fury; the wrathful man of Proverbs 15:18 is literally a man of heat.
Hebrew erek appayim (H750, H639) — long of nostrils, slow to anger; the opposite figure in the same verse, and a title of God in Exodus 34:6.
Greek orge (G3709) — settled indignation, as distinct from thumos (G2372), a passion that boils and subsides.
Saxon wraeth, from writhan — to writhe; Webster's root, the body inside the word.
usage: “Let thy wrathful anger take hold of them” — the petition hands the case upward.
“A wrathful man stirreth up strife” — it makes conflict, never justice.
“The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” — not rarely; not.

pos: a. (not deserving; wanting merit or worth; unbecoming)
etymology: From worthy, Saxon weorth, value, price, with the negative prefix. To be unworthy is to lack the price that would answer for the thing — a commercial figure carried into the moral realm.
biblical_def: The two occurrences pull in opposite directions and both are instructive. The first is a self-verdict with eternal weight: “It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles” (Act 13:46). Paul does not say God judged them unworthy; he says they judged themselves so, by putting the word from them. Rejection of the gospel is itself the verdict, and no other sentence has to be pronounced. The second is a rebuke to false modesty: “Do ye not know that the saints shall judge the world? and if the world shall be judged by you, are ye unworthy to judge the smallest matters?” (1Co 6:2). The Corinthians were hauling each other before pagan courts while pleading incompetence to settle their own disputes, and Paul calls the plea what it is. So Scripture forbids two things at once: presuming worth one does not have, and disclaiming a competence God has actually given. The prodigal supplies the sound version — “I am no more worthy to be called thy son” (Luk 15:19) — spoken on the way home, not as a reason to stay away. And Paul warns that the Table itself may be approached unworthily (1Co 11:27), which is a manner of coming, not a class of person.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unworthy as not deserving; wanting merit or worth; and also unbecoming, as conduct unworthy of a Christian.
webster_full: UNWOR'THY, a.
1. Not deserving; followed by of. He is unworthy of our regard.
2. Wanting merit or worth; worthless; base.
3. Unbecoming; vile; shameful; as conduct unworthy of a man of honor.
4. Not suitable; inadequate. Ye judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life. Acts 13. From weorth, value or price.
scriptures: Acts 13:46

Then Paul and Barnabas waxed bold, and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.
1 Corinthians 6:2
Do ye not know that the saints shall judge the world? and if the world shall be judged by you, are ye unworthy to judge the smallest matters?
1 Corinthians 11:27
Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.
Luke 15:19
And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants.
corruption_summary: Unworthiness is treated as a wound to be healed rather than a fact to be confessed, and so the one road to the Father's house is closed off as unhealthy.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic register has classified feelings of unworthiness as a disorder, and much preaching has obliged by assuring congregations of their inherent worth. Luke 15:19 puts the confession in the mouth of the returning son and treats it as the mark that he has come to himself. He is not wallowing; he is walking. The father's embrace does not correct his self-assessment — it overrules its consequences. That is the gospel's actual comfort, and it is stronger than the assurance it has been traded for: not you were worthy all along, but you were not, and you are received.

At the Table the corruption runs the other way, and it keeps tender consciences from the ordinance for years. 1 Corinthians 11:27 says unworthily — an adverb. Paul is describing a manner of eating, specifically the Corinthian practice of humiliating the poor at the supper, not erecting a standard of personal worthiness no communicant could meet. The Reformed churches have always taught that the Table is for sinners who examine themselves, not for the worthy; a man who came worthy would not need it. Acts 13:46 then gives the one unworthiness that is fatal, and it is not a feeling at all: putting the word from you.
roots_summary: Greek anaxios (G370), unworthy, not of like weight; axios (G514), of weight, worthy; Saxon weorth, value or price.
roots_lines: Greek ouk axious (G514) — not worthy; Acts 13:46, a verdict the hearers pass on themselves.
Greek anaxioi (G370) — unworthy, incompetent; 1 Corinthians 6:2, of judging the smallest matters.
Greek anaxios (G371) as adverb — unworthily; 1 Corinthians 11:27, a manner of eating, not a class of person.
Greek axios (G514) — literally bringing up the scale, of like weight; the commercial figure under the moral word.
Saxon weorth — value, price; Webster's root, the same picture of a weight that answers.
usage: “Judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life” — the rejection is the sentence.
“Are ye unworthy to judge the smallest matters?” — false modesty called what it is.
“I am no more worthy to be called thy son” — said on the road home, not as a reason to stay away.
